summary: This unit teaches you to look after a salon or spa's stock: order what is needed, receive and check deliveries, store products safely (including chemicals and flammables), rotate stock first in, first out, keep stock records, count stock and work out its value, deal with damaged and out-of-date items, reduce losses and keep the stock room safe and tidy.

blocks.p: A salon or spa buys products and supplies with its own money. Stock that is lost, spoiled, expired or never used is money wasted; stock that runs out means clients are turned away and services cannot be done. Stock control is the set of habits that keeps the right amount of the right goods, in good condition, in the right place. This unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and applies in a hair salon, a nail bar and a day spa.

Stock control is also a **safety** job. Relaxers, peroxide, acetone and hairspray can burn, poison or catch fire if they are stored or handled wrongly. A tidy, well-organised stock room protects people as well as money.

sections.title: Kinds of stock and where it comes from

head: Kind of stock
What it is
Examples
rows: Retail stock
Products sold to clients to use at home.
Shampoo, conditioner, leave-in, cuticle oil, hand cream, sunscreen, nail polish
Professional (back-bar) stock
Products used by staff on clients during services.
Relaxer, hair colour, peroxide, salon-size shampoo, wax, massage oil
Consumables
Items used up and replaced often.
Cotton wool, gloves, neck strips, tissues, foils, cotton pads, nail files
Linen
Towels, gowns and capes; washed and reused but wear out.
Towels, cutting capes, robes
Equipment and tools
Items used for years but kept in good order.
Scissors, clippers, steamers, dryers, trolleys

blocks.p: Count towels and gowns too: they get lost, stained or worn and need replacing in time. Consumables run out fastest, so check them most often.

head: Word
Meaning
rows: Supplier (wholesaler, distributor)
The business that sells stock to the salon.
Catalogue or price list
A list of the supplier's products, codes and prices.
Purchase order
A form the salon sends to a supplier to order goods: what, how many and at what price.
Delivery note
A list from the supplier of the goods sent in that delivery.
Invoice
The supplier's bill, asking the salon to pay for the goods.
Stock card (bin card)
A card for one item that records each item received, used or sold, and the balance left.
Lead time
The time between placing an order and the goods arriving.
Barcode
The label of black stripes and numbers that is scanned at the till to identify a product.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, deliveries can be late in bad weather or at busy seasons such as Christmas and graduation. Allow for the lead time when you plan an order, and keep a small safety stock of the items you cannot do without.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Level
What it is
Why it matters
rows: Maximum stock
The most of an item the salon wants to hold at one time.
Stops money being tied up, space filling and products expiring.
Minimum (safety) stock
The smallest amount to hold, so the salon does not run out if a delivery is late or sales rise.
Protects services and sales.
Reorder level
The stock level at which a new order is placed.
Orders go in early enough to arrive before stock runs out.

blocks.p: **Reorder level = (usage per week x lead time in weeks) + safety stock.**

head: Example
Working
rows: A spa uses 4 tubs of wax a week. A delivery takes 2 weeks. Safety stock is 3 tubs.
4 x 2 = 8; 8 + 3 = **11 tubs**. Order when stock falls to 11.
A salon uses 5 tubs of hair food a week, lead time 2 weeks, safety stock 4.
Maximum 30 tubs; 14 on hand when the order is placed.
Order 30 - 14 = 16 tubs.
Maximum 40 bottles; 14 on the shelf.
Order 40 - 14 = 26 bottles.
3 bottles of peroxide a week for 8 weeks.
3 x 8 = 24 bottles.
1,200 gloves needed; boxes of 100.

head: Problem
Effect
rows: Overstocking (too much)
Money is tied up; products may expire before use; space is wasted; more risk of theft and damage.
Understocking (too little)
The salon runs out; services or sales are lost; clients go elsewhere; rush orders cost more.

flow: Check stock levels and how fast each item is used
Check the budget and what is already on order
List items and quantities; check the catalogue for codes and prices
Fill in the purchase order
Get the supervisor or manager who controls the budget to agree it
Send it to the supplier and keep a copy
Note the expected delivery date

blocks.note: Check the stock record, not only a quick look at the shelf. Items hidden at the back can be missed, and a quick look can order what you already have.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Usage records:** note what is used (especially professional products like colour and peroxide), so you can predict what to order.
**Seasonal demand:** before Christmas, graduation and carnival, more clients come; order early.
Order the pack size you can use before the expiry date: a large tub of a slow-moving product may expire half full.

flow: Check the delivery is for the salon and find your copy of the purchase order
Count the boxes and look for crushed, wet or leaking packages before you sign
Open the boxes and check each item against the delivery note and the purchase order: product, size, colour, number
Check expiry dates and that seals are not broken
Write any shortage, wrong item or damage on the delivery note before you sign; keep damaged items apart
Tell the supervisor so the supplier can be contacted
Enter the goods received on the stock cards or the computer system
Put the stock away safely: new behind old; chemicals in their proper store

head: Problem found
What to do
rows: Delivery note says 24 tubes of colour; only 20 in the box
Record the shortage on the delivery note, tell the supervisor and the supplier.
Wrong product or size sent
Keep it apart; record; report; do not add it to stock until the supervisor decides.
Crushed, leaking box (e.g. nail polish remover)
Put on gloves, keep it apart, record the damage and report it. Mop up any spill using the safety data sheet.
Out of date or nearly out of date
Do not accept it as good stock; record and report.
Broken seal or tampering
Do not use; record and report.
Extra items not ordered
Record and report; do not add to stock.

blocks.p: **Why check expiry dates at delivery?** So you do not accept stock that is out of date or nearly so. Look for the date or the open-jar symbol on the pack.

blocks.note: Do not sign for goods you have not checked. Your signature says the delivery was complete and in good order, and it is hard to claim from a supplier afterwards. If you cannot check at once, write 'not checked' on the note beside your signature.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: Lift boxes with a straight back and bent knees; share heavy loads.
Open boxes with a safety cutter, cutting away from your body.
Use a trolley for heavy deliveries. Keep walkways clear of boxes.

blocks.p: The invoice is the supplier's bill. The person who pays checks the invoice against the delivery note and the purchase order before paying: the goods ordered, received and billed must match, at the agreed price.

head: Rule
Why
rows: Store products in a cool, dry, clean place out of direct sunlight, away from water heaters and dryers.
Heat and sun spoil products, make them separate or lose strength; aerosols can burst. This matters in Jamaica's heat.
Heavy items and large bottles on the lower shelves.
Safe to lift; they cannot fall.
Keep products in their original, labelled containers with lids closed.
The label shows the contents, hazards and safe use.
Do not pour products into unlabelled or food and drink bottles.
Someone could swallow or misuse them.
Keep the stock room tidy with clear walkways, shelves not overloaded.
Stock is easy to find and count; nobody trips.
Keep a fire extinguisher close and know how to use it.
Fire safety.
Store towels and gowns clean and dry in a closed cupboard.
Damp linen grows mould.

ul: Relaxers, perm lotion, hair colour and **peroxide** are kept in their original containers, as the **safety data sheet (SDS)** says.
The SDS from the maker tells you how to store the chemical safely, what hazards it has, what to wear and what to do if it spills or splashes.
Keep chemicals in a **locked store or cupboard**, away from children and people who are not trained, and below eye level.
Never mix two chemicals or cleaners together; some give off poisonous gas.
Do not store chemicals near heat or food.

blocks.p: **Flammable** products catch fire easily. They include acetone, nail polish and polish remover, hairspray and some alcohol-based products. A label with a flame symbol warns you that the product is flammable.

ul: Store in a cool, **ventilated** place **away from heat, flames and sparks**: heaters, dryers, cookers, sockets.
No smoking or naked flames near them.
Keep lids tightly closed; keep only small amounts at the workstation.
Keep a fire extinguisher close.

blocks.note: If peroxide splashes into a worker's eye, rinse it at once with lots of clean running water and get medical help. Read the SDS for the product for first aid.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Stock
Where and how
rows: Retail products
On display or in the stock room; cool, dry, out of the sun; testers separate.
Hair colour and peroxide
Locked cupboard; cool; originals; lids closed; labelled.
Relaxers and perm lotion
Locked cupboard; cool; away from acid products; as the SDS says.
Acetone, polish, hairspray
Cool, ventilated; away from heat and flames.
Towels and gowns
Clean, dry, closed cupboard.
Gloves and consumables
Clean, dry shelf; keep dust off.
Single-use sharps, blades
Sharps box; never loose.

sections.title: Stock rotation, stock records and usage

blocks.p: **FIFO** means **first in, first out**: the older stock is used or sold first. Beauty products lose their quality over time, so rotation stops stock going out of date on the shelf, saves money, and means clients get fresh, safe products.

flow: When a delivery arrives, check the dates on the stock already on the shelf
Move the older items to the front
Put the new items behind them, or underneath in the stock room
If a new item has an earlier expiry date, it goes to the front
Remove items that are out of date or damaged and record them

blocks.p: Example: new bottles of shampoo go behind the older bottles, so the older ones sell first.
A **stock card** (bin card) is kept for each item. It records each item received, used or sold, and the balance left.

head: Date
Received
Used or sold
Balance
rows: 1 Nov
20 bottles
3 Nov
5 Nov

blocks.p: Balance = old balance + received - used or sold. Here 20 + 12 = 32; 32 - 7 = **25 bottles**. Keep stock records up to date every day, so the salon knows what it has and when to reorder.

head: System
Good points
Weak points
rows: Paper stock cards
Cheap and simple.
Slow; mistakes in adding are easy.
Computer or tablet system
Takes an item off the count when it is sold at the till; prints reports; warns at reorder level.
Costs money; needs power and training; cannot see theft or damage, so counts of the shelves are still needed.

blocks.p: What each record should show: product name and code, supplier, date, quantity in and out, balance, reorder level and cost price.

ul: Professional products are used on clients and not sold, so they are easily wasted.
Follow the maker's amounts; measure with pumps, cups or scales; mix only what is needed for the client.
Take one bottle out of the stock room at a time and finish it before opening another.
Record each item taken from stock on the stock card or system. Colour use can be noted on the client's record.
Close lids so products do not spill or dry out.
Why? Recording how much professional product is used for each client controls waste, helps cost each service and shows when to reorder.

blocks.note: When a stylist takes a bottle of conditioner from the stock room to use at the basin, she records it as used stock on the stock card or system. Unrecorded stock cannot be told from missing stock.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **stock take** is counting all the stock and comparing it with the records. Do it at a quiet time or when the salon is closed, so that sales and deliveries do not upset the count.

flow: Plan the stock take; give each person a stock sheet for an area
Count shelf by shelf, in order, and write each number down at once
A second person checks some of the counts
Count damaged and out-of-date items separately
Compare the counts with the stock cards or system
Recheck any difference (variance)
Work out the value of the stock
Correct the records; report results and losses to the manager

blocks.p: A **variance** is the difference between the count and the record. If the count is less than the record, there is a **shortage**; if more, an **overage**.

head: Example
Working
rows: Card says 30 jars; count finds 27
30 - 27 = **shortage of 3 jars**
Card says 12; count finds 14
Overage of 2: check for a missed entry

blocks.p: Value = number of items x cost price. Use the **cost price** (what the salon paid), not the selling price.

head: Item
Count
Cost each
Value
rows: Body lotion
Hair food
Nail files (5 packs of a dozen)
60 files
Total

blocks.p: Nail files come in packs of a dozen, so 5 packs hold 5 x 12 = 60 files.

blocks.note: Open items used at the basin may be counted as part bottles, as the salon's method says. Items past their date are counted but not included in the value of good stock.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: A computer system is not a substitute for a count. It cannot see losses and mistakes such as theft, breakage or the wrong item scanned. Count the shelves regularly even if you have a system.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Use a proper step stool, not a chair or a box, for high shelves.
Do not open chemical containers.
Put each item back where it came from, with heavy items low.
Keep walkways clear of boxes.

flow: Take the item off the shelf or out of use straight away
If it is leaking or broken, put on gloves, clean up as the safety data sheet says, and put out a wet floor sign
Keep it in a marked box or area for damaged stock
Record it: date, product, number and reason
Report it to the supervisor
Return it to the supplier for credit if possible, or dispose of it as the maker's instructions and local rules say
Correct the stock records

ul: **Out-of-date products must never be used on clients.** They may not work and may irritate or harm the skin. A jar of facial cream past its date is removed, recorded and disposed of as the policy says.
Chemicals, such as leftover mixed hair colour, are disposed of as the maker's instructions and the local rules say. They are never poured on the ground or down a drain not meant for them.

blocks.h: A spill in the stock room

flow: Warn others and keep them away; ventilate the room
Read the safety data sheet
Put on gloves, eye protection and an apron
Pick up broken glass with a dustpan, not your hands, into a strong marked container
Soak up the liquid as the SDS says; wipe the area with water
Put out a wet floor sign
Dispose of the waste as the SDS and local rules say
Record and report it

blocks.note: If any chemical touches skin or eyes, rinse with plenty of clean running water and get medical help.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: **Shrinkage** is stock the salon has paid for but lost, so it is never sold or used properly.

head: Cause
How to reduce it
rows: Theft by clients or staff
Keep most retail stock in a locked cabinet or stock room; display testers only.
Damage
Store and handle stock carefully; heavy items low.
Expiry
Rotate stock; order sensible amounts.
Waste
Measure products; mix only what is needed.
Mistakes in counting or records
Record every item taken or received; regular counts; deliveries checked.

blocks.p: If stock keeps going missing from the stock room, report it to the supervisor or manager as the salon's procedure says. Do not accuse anyone yourself.

blocks.note: Never take stock home or use it for yourself without the owner's permission and a record. Taking stock without permission is theft, even for a small item.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: A safe, tidy stock room, and revision

ul: Keep it clean and tidy so stock is easy to find and count, and nobody trips or is hurt.
Keep walkways and the door clear; do not stack boxes against the fire exit.
Do not overload shelves; heavy items go on the bottom.
Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet floor sign.
Know where the fire extinguisher, first-aid kit and safety data sheets are.
Wash your hands after handling chemicals; wear gloves and eye protection when the SDS says.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's hot weather, keep the stock room ventilated and out of the sun. Check for mould on damp towels and for signs of pests: keep food out of the stock room, and report any problem.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can name the kinds of stock: retail, professional, consumables, linen and equipment.
I can explain a purchase order, delivery note, invoice, stock card and lead time.
I can explain maximum, minimum and reorder levels, and work out a reorder level.
I can say why overstocking and understocking are both a problem.
I can fill in a purchase order and get it agreed.
I can receive a delivery: check damage, quantities and dates, record problems and report them.
I can store products in a cool, dry place with heavy items low and labels showing.
I can store chemicals and flammables as the safety data sheet says.
I can rotate stock first in, first out.
I can keep stock cards and work out the balance.
I can record professional product use and say why.
I can carry out a stock take, find variances and work out stock values.
I can deal with damaged and out-of-date stock and a spill in the stock room.
I can name the causes of shrinkage and say how to reduce it.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I put new stock behind the old, so that the older products are sold before they expire.'
blocks.label: Tip

A supplier's list of products, codes and prices.
The time between placing an order and the goods arriving.
A record for one item: received, used or sold, and balance.

The stock level at which a new order is placed.

c1.title: A delivery at the back door in May Pen
c1.text: A van delivers an order to a salon and spa in May Pen. The purchase order lists 30 bottles of shampoo, 24 tubs of hair food and 12 bottles of acetone. The driver is in a hurry and holds out the delivery note for a signature. Trainee Rashane notices one carton is wet at the bottom, with a strong smell of acetone. The delivery note shows 24 tubs of hair food, but only 20 are in the carton.

c2.title: A messy stock room in Lucea
c2.text: The stock room of a salon in Lucea is a small, hot room with no window. Boxes of acetone and hairspray are stacked beside the water heater. A large carton of peroxide bottles is on the top shelf, above a shelf of relaxers. New stock of conditioner has been placed in front of older bottles, and the older bottles are near their expiry date. A bottle of colour has been poured into an unlabelled soda bottle.

c3.title: Ordering wax for the spa in Port Antonio
c3.text: A day spa in Port Antonio uses 6 tubs of wax a week. The supplier delivers 3 weeks after an order. The spa keeps 4 tubs of safety stock and never wants more than 36 tubs on the premises. At the moment the stock card shows 15 tubs.

c4.title: A stock take in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: On Monday morning, when the spa is closed, trainees Dwight and Kimberly do a stock take. The stock card says there should be 40 jars of body butter, each costing J$900. They count 36 jars. They also find 4 jars of facial cream past their expiry date, and notice that over the last month stock of nail polish has gone missing from an unlocked display cabinet.

c5.title: Colour use and waste in Montego Bay
c5.text: A salon in Montego Bay finds that its hair colour stock is running out much faster than the number of colour services explains. Stylists take two or three tubes at a time from the stock room, mix large amounts, and throw away what is left. Nobody writes down what is taken.

questions.q: What should Rashane do before signing the delivery note?
o: Sign now so that the driver can leave, and check the load later on
Check the cartons and items against the note and order, and write down problems
Send the driver away with the whole delivery still on the van, until the supervisor is back
Sign, and ask the supplier to come back and count the goods for her later
questions.why: Your signature says the delivery was complete and in good order. Check the cartons for damage, check each item against the delivery note and the purchase order, and write problems on the note before you sign.

questions.q: What should be done about the wet carton that smells of acetone?
o: Put on gloves, keep it apart, record the damage and report it
Put it in the stock room with the others and let it dry out
Open it in the salon so that clients can see what is inside
Pour the leaking bottle into a clean one and store it again
questions.why: A leaking container of a flammable chemical is a hazard. Wear gloves, keep it away from other stock and from flames or heat, ventilate, record it and report it so the supplier can be contacted. Never transfer it to another container.

questions.q: The note lists 24 tubs of hair food, but only 20 are in the carton. What should Rashane do?
o: Enter 24 tubs on the stock card, as the delivery note says
Throw away the note and enter nothing on the stock card at all
Enter 20, and tell the supervisor and supplier about the shortage
Ask the driver to leave 4 tubs from another customer's order
questions.why: Record what was really received, write the shortage on the delivery note and tell the supervisor so the supplier can send the missing four or give a credit. The stock card must show the true balance.

questions.q: After the delivery is checked, where should the 12 bottles of acetone be stored?
o: Beside the dryers, where they will be used most often by the stylists
In a cool, ventilated place away from heat, flames and sparks
In the sun, so that they stay dry and ready for use when they are needed
Next to the peroxide, since both of them are chemicals used in the salon
questions.why: Acetone is flammable: store it cool, ventilated and away from heat, flames and sparks. Chemicals that can react with each other are not stored together.

questions.q: What is the most serious fire risk in the stock room?
o: The conditioner that has been placed in front of the older bottles
Acetone and hairspray boxes stacked beside the water heater
The unlabelled soda bottle standing on the shelf
The wet patch of floor near the door of the stock room
questions.why: Acetone and hairspray are flammable and aerosols can burst with heat. They belong in a cool, ventilated place away from heaters, sparks and flames.

questions.q: Why is storing the carton of peroxide on the top shelf above the relaxers a problem?
o: Peroxide must always be stored at floor level, and never on any shelf above it
Relaxers must be kept in direct light so that they stay stable on the shelf
Shelves above head height are only meant for light, empty boxes and packaging
A fall or leak would spill onto the chemicals below, and the carton is heavy
questions.why: Heavy items belong on the lower shelves so they are safe to lift and cannot fall, and chemicals that react should not be stored where a leak could mix them. Store each as its safety data sheet says.

questions.q: What is wrong with the colour poured into an unlabelled soda bottle?
o: The soda bottle will crack from the chemical inside it after a short time
The colour will go off in plastic after only a few days of being stored
It could be swallowed or misused, and the label's warnings are lost
The bottle is too large and tall to fit on the shelf with the other products
questions.why: Products must stay in their original, labelled containers. A drink bottle invites someone to drink it, and without the label nobody knows the contents, hazards or first aid.

questions.q: How should the new and older bottles of conditioner be arranged?
o: Newest in front, so that clients see the freshest bottles first
Oldest in front, with new bottles behind, using first in, first out
In order of price, with the cheapest bottles at the front
Mixed together so that no one date stands out on the shelf
questions.why: Stock rotation (FIFO) puts the older stock at the front so it is used or sold before it expires; new stock goes behind or underneath.

questions.q: How many tubs of wax will the spa use while it waits for an order to arrive?
o: 6 tubs
12 tubs
18 tubs
22 tubs
questions.why: Usage during the lead time = 6 tubs a week x 3 weeks = 18 tubs. Add the 4 tubs of safety stock and the reorder level is 22 tubs.

questions.q: The stock card shows 15 tubs. What should the spa do?
o: Order now, because stock is already below the reorder level
Wait until stock falls as low as the safety stock of 4 tubs
Order only when the very last tub has been opened
Do nothing at all, since the maximum is 36 tubs
questions.why: 15 is below the reorder level of 22, and the order takes 3 weeks to arrive, so stock could run out before it comes. Order now.

questions.q: How many tubs should the spa order to bring stock up to its maximum of 36?
o: 15 tubs
21 tubs
22 tubs
36 tubs
questions.why: Maximum minus stock on hand: 36 - 15 = 21 tubs.

questions.q: Wax is sold in tubs, and the spa decides to order a larger pack of a slow-selling scent. What is the main risk?
o: The scent may turn out to be too strong for some clients
The large pack may expire half full, tying up the spa's money
Large packs can never be rotated on the shelf or in the store
Orders must always be placed for the smallest pack size
questions.why: Overstocking a slow-moving item ties up money, and the product may reach its expiry date before it is used. Order pack sizes you can use in time.

questions.q: What does the count of 36 jars, against 40 on the stock card, show?
o: A shortage of 4 jars
An overage of 4 jars
A shortage of 36 jars
Nothing, since the card is always right
questions.why: The count is less than the record: 40 - 36 = 4 jars short. The difference is rechecked and the cause looked for.

questions.q: What is the value of the 36 jars of body butter at J$900 cost each?
questions.why: Value = number x cost price: 36 x J$900 = J$32,400.

questions.q: What should Dwight and Kimberly do with the four expired jars of facial cream?
o: Use them up on staff members before they get any older or go off
Remove them, record them and dispose of them as the policy says
Sell them at a discount to clients who ask for a bargain price
Put them at the back of the shelf behind the newer stock for now
questions.why: Out-of-date products may not work and can irritate or harm the skin, so they are never used on clients or sold. Remove, record and dispose as the policy and local rules say.

questions.q: How could the spa reduce the loss of nail polish from the display cabinet?
o: Keep most stock locked away and put only testers on display
Remove all price tickets from the polish
Count the polish only once a year
Keep the cabinet unlocked so that clients can browse easily
questions.why: Keeping the stock in a locked cabinet or the stock room, with testers on show, reduces theft. Regular counts and records also help find losses early.

questions.q: What is the main reason the colour stock is running out so fast?
o: The supplier has been sending short deliveries to the salon for some months
Colour tubes dry up in the stock room when the room gets hot in the afternoon
Clients have been taking tubes of colour home with them without telling anyone
Stylists take too much, mix too much and record nothing, so waste is hidden
questions.why: Professional products are easily wasted when staff take more than needed, mix large amounts and keep no record. Without records, waste cannot be told from theft or mistakes.

questions.q: Which change would best control the use of colour?
o: Measure the mix for each client, take one tube at a time and record it
Lock the stock room and give the key to every stylist in the salon
Ban hair colour services until the next stock take has been done
Allow stylists to take whatever they need without writing it down
questions.why: Measuring, mixing only what is needed, opening one container at a time and recording use controls waste, costs each service and shows when to reorder.

questions.q: A stock card opens at 50 tubs of hair food. Over the week, 14 are used, 20 are delivered, and 11 more are used. What is the balance?
o: 35 tubs
45 tubs

questions.q: A worker finds that stock has been going missing from the stock room for several weeks. What should she do?
o: Search her co-workers' bags and tell them off in front of clients
Report it to the supervisor or manager, as the procedure says
Say nothing in case it is only a counting mistake
Hide the stock in a different cupboard so nobody can take it
questions.why: Report losses to the supervisor or manager, who can investigate under the salon's procedure. Do not accuse anyone yourself or search others' belongings.
